meta.title: Start with connection
meta.sub: Help children from 12 months through age 6 before, during and after a difficult feeling.

meta.title: Make the day easier to manage
meta.sub: Show what happens next, make busy routines easier and offer a quieter place with adult help.

meta.title: Respond before distress grows
meta.sub: Notice when help is needed, respect a child’s “no” to touch and respond to requests for help or a break.

meta.title: Keep everyone safe, then reconnect
meta.sub: Know when to get urgent help, keep children supervised and offer comfort after danger has passed.

meta.title: Teach skills in everyday play
meta.sub: Show one useful action in play, help the child use it in the day and stop when play becomes uncomfortable.

meta.title: Build the plan together
meta.sub: Use clear observations and family knowledge to agree what adults will try and when to ask for more help.

practice.q: Fourteen-month-old Imani reaches towards a familiar adult. When two adults speak at once and a musical toy starts, she turns away, pushes it aside and fusses. She mainly uses gestures and sounds. What should the adult do?
o: Offer a different toy and continue the familiar song.
Stop the toy and extra talk, offer familiar comfort and check what care or help she needs.
Show a new help picture and ask her to point before deciding what to do.
practice.why: Imani is already showing that she may need a pause. Reduce sound, offer familiar comfort and check care needs. Watch before showing one simple next step. Like Amira, she needs help; she is not expected to explain a feeling or solve a problem.

practice.q: Three-year-old Leo covers his ears as chairs scrape and children crowd the tidy-up shelf. He backs away and mostly uses gestures. What would help first?
o: Explain a breathing picture while the room stays the same.
Take him to a feelings display to choose a word before helping.
Reduce noise and crowding, stay with him in a quieter spot and use a familiar gesture or object to show one next step.
practice.why: Fewer children at the shelf and less chair noise change the difficult situation. A picture alone does not. Later, check which gestures Leo uses and whether staff made the changes and he could comfortably reach the next activity.

practice.q: Two-year-old Priya finds a different adult at arrival. She clings to her caregiver, turns away and pushes aside the adult’s hand. What should happen next?
o: Offer a cuddle instead and explain that the adult can help.
Give her space, stay nearby with few words and follow the arrival routine agreed with the family.
Teach two new ways to calm down so she can choose.
practice.why: Priya can decline touch and still need company. Stop the touch, keep care and supervision in place and use the known arrival routine. Plan for an absent familiar adult with the family and teacher.

practice.q: Five-year-old Ben lifts a chair while upset after a game ends. Children are nearby and another adult is available. What should guide the first response?
o: Give a longer explanation and send the colleague for a feelings chart.
Practise a calming routine before involving other staff.
Call the agreed trained help, keep children supervised and help create safe space under school procedures.
practice.why: Protect people and get the right help before teaching. The safe action depends on the room and current procedures. This course does not teach or authorise holding techniques. Practise the staff conversation, never the dangerous behaviour.

practice.q: Four-year-old Sofia uses a help card during a calm lesson. At snack, her lid is stuck. She cries and pushes the box away; the card is in a drawer. What should staff do?
o: Help now, then put the familiar card at snack, show its use during easy practice and make sure adults respond.
Fetch the card and repeat the lesson before opening the box.
Replace it with several new cards and ask which she prefers.
practice.why: Sofia is already showing she needs help. Open the box without waiting for the right card response. Later, put the card where it is needed and show a substitute adult how to respond. Check whether Sofia can get help and eat her snack.

practice.q: Five-year-old Noah moves away during large-group singing. His caregiver says he sings at home. Which opening would help staff and family make a useful plan?
o: “We’ll practise naming feelings more often, then see if he joins.”
“He enjoys chosen songs in a small group here, but moves away in the large group. What helps at home? Could we try a quieter place with an adult nearby and compare how he feels and joins in?”
“We’ll count how often he leaves to decide whether the plan works.”
practice.why: Start with a strength, describe what you saw and ask the family. Agree who makes the change and when to review. Check whether it happened and whether Noah was comfortable and able to enjoy singing. Seek help sooner for growing health, safety or child-protection concerns.

declarations: I will treat an upset child with dignity, use communication they understand and offer calm adult help while keeping people safe.
I will adapt routines and tasks to the child’s needs, including communication, sound, touch and movement, and teach when they can join in.
I will not shame, threaten or isolate a child, force eye contact or affection, or withhold necessary care to make them do something.
I will follow current school safeguarding, supervision and emergency procedures, get trained help and stay within my role. This course does not teach or permit restraint.
I understand this certificate records online learning only. I will use approved school systems for real concerns, support plans and family messages, never this course.

localReadiness.title: Know this child
localReadiness.text: Ask the teacher about the child’s usual gestures, words, interests, comfort and care plan. These examples start at 12 months; ages are planning guides, not tests. Anyone giving personal care also needs the school’s approved handling, care and rest/sleep training.

localReadiness.title: Know who can help you
localReadiness.text: Agree how to call for help, who stays with the child and who watches the group. Name a backup. Practise asking and waiting for a clear reply before handing over; do not simply walk away.

localReadiness.title: Check the room and routine
localReadiness.text: Look for noisy chairs, crowded shelves or long waits. Show a familiar picture or object where it is needed, what happens next and a change of plan. Check quieter places, safe exits, age-safe resources and who stays nearby, including when the usual spot is occupied.

localReadiness.title: Agree how adults respond
localReadiness.text: Know what happens when a child asks for help or a break. Practise a few words and a pause. Be ready to offer space or another support if touch or a tool is declined. Care must not depend on speaking, eye contact, breathing or looking calm.

localReadiness.title: Know urgent help and reporting routes
localReadiness.text: Find the teacher or inclusion/ELS lead for extra support, the safeguarding lead for child-protection concerns, the alternative reporting route and the first-aid/emergency process. Urgent danger needs help now.

localReadiness.title: Review with the family
localReadiness.text: Write what you saw separately from possible explanations, using approved secure records. Check what adults changed and whether the child could ask for help, feel comfortable and enjoy activities. Agree who reviews with the family and when. Ask for advice sooner if concerns grow.

practical.title: Practise helping a child together
practical.intro: For adults supporting children from 12 months through age 6. Use fictional examples with a colleague, or say both adult roles aloud. Co-regulation means helping a child through a difficult feeling with calm adult support. This guide supports practice and discussion; completing the online course does not prove practical skill.
instructions: Read this example first: at tidy-up, Leo covers his ears. One adult agrees to watch the group; another stays nearby. Staff reduce noise and send fewer children to the shelf. The adult shows Leo his familiar basket: “One block here,” then shows the next activity. If he needs a pause, they stay together in the agreed quieter spot.

Choose Imani’s arrival at 14 months, Priya’s arrival, Leo’s tidy-up, Sofia’s snack or Noah’s singing. Say how the child shows what they need. For example, Imani turns away and pushes the noisy toy aside; the adult stops it and checks care needs.

Agree who speaks, who watches the group and how to get help. Show your words, a familiar object/picture/sign and one change, such as fewer children at the shelf. Never act out aggression, practise restraint or rehearse handling a child from this course.

Your partner adds a change: touch is declined, a picture is missing, the quieter seat is occupied or the usual adult is absent. Show another way to help. Anyone can pause the practice. If alone, describe both adults’ actions.

Use the checks below. Name one action that helped and one to improve. With the teacher or relevant lead, agree a safe small change to try and when to review it through supervised practice. Keep real children’s details out of this course and use approved secure records.

items: Shows a known object or picture while doing the step, then shows what comes next. For example: show the tidy-up basket, say “One block here,” then show the next activity. If the shelf is blocked, show the real alternative.
Changes something practical, such as fewer children at the shelf, and identifies another safe place with adult support if the quieter spot is occupied.
Matches help to the child: familiar comfort and one simple step for 12 months to under 18 months; practical help for an older toddler; a next step the older child can manage.

criteria.area: 2. Offer help the child can use
items: Says what they notice, uses a few warm words, pauses and gives the child space.
Accepts the child’s gesture, sign, picture, device or words. Shows the actual help or break that follows.
Stops an unwanted offer of touch, breathing or a tool and offers another way to help. Care, supervision and adult company remain available.
Asks a colleague for a clear job, waits for agreement and shares what happened, what helped and who watches each group.
Can find the current safety, first-aid/emergency and safeguarding routes, including backups, and say when urgent help is needed.
Keeps practice non-physical and within role limits. Does not practise restraint, locking a child away, forced isolation, humiliation or withholding care.

criteria.area: 4. Teach later and check what helped
items: Offers a supported return without requiring an apology, explanation or repair first. Helps put things right later, when the child is ready.
Shows one useful action in comfortable play, offers a turn without pressure and puts the familiar support in the real routine with an adult ready to respond.
Keeps facts and guesses separate, names what an adult will change and who will review it, and checks the child’s comfort, communication and enjoyment with the family.

decisionOptions: Agree one small change and a review date
Ask the relevant school lead before changing the child’s plan
practical.footer: Use this guide for discussion, coaching and supervised practice. It is not permission to carry out a procedure or proof of professional competence. The school must approve individual plans and role responsibilities and provide required care, safeguarding and safety training.

visualGuides.title: Be the steady adult
visualGuides.intro: A child’s tower falls and blocks scatter. Check safety, offer company and make one small next step easier. The child does not have to work through a fixed set of stages.

steps.title: Notice yourself
steps.text: Is your voice getting faster or sharper? Notice tense hands. Take a brief pause if it is safe.

steps.title: Use a steadier voice
steps.text: Slow your next sentence and lower your volume: “That fell down. I can stay here.”

steps.title: Stay nearby without pressure
steps.text: Give the child comfortable space. Offer company without insisting on touch or eye contact.

steps.title: Make one thing easier
steps.text: Move the audience on or offer one block together. Offer only choices you can provide; the child may prefer a break.

steps.title: Ask for clear help
steps.text: “Can you watch the group? I’ll stay with Amira.” Wait for agreement. Before handing over, share what happened, what helped and who is supervising.

visualGuides.title: Less pressure, more help
visualGuides.intro: A child covers their ears and moves away as the class lines up. Make the line less crowded and offer a quieter place with an adult nearby.

steps.title: Notice what you see
steps.text: Hands cover ears; the child backs away or uses fewer words. Describe these actions without guessing why.

steps.title: Change the difficult part
steps.text: Reduce noise and crowding. With the teacher, arrange a quieter waiting place or let smaller groups move at a time. Keep supervision clear.

steps.title: Say a few words, then wait
steps.text: You might say, “It’s noisy. I’m here. We can wait here together.” Give the child time to understand or respond.

steps.title: Respond to the child’s message
steps.text: Accept their usual help or break gesture, picture or device. Show the actual help. If the usual seat is occupied, offer another safe place with adult support.

steps.title: Watch and adjust
steps.text: If touch or a tool is declined, stop that offer, give space and remain available. Use the school’s safety or health response immediately if risk or a health concern grows.

visualGuides.title: Keep helping after the difficult moment
visualGuides.intro: A child is quiet after an upsetting event. Check comfort and care first. They can return to play with help before discussing or putting things right.

steps.title: Keep care and company available
steps.text: Keep the child supervised, reduce noise or pressure and meet care needs. Comfort is not a reward to remove.

steps.title: Offer familiar support
steps.text: Offer a known toy, company or space. A child may not want breathing, touch or talking; offer another way to help.

steps.title: Look for interest, without rushing
steps.text: Watch for the child’s usual signs of comfort or interest in play. Silence alone does not mean they are ready for questions.

steps.title: Help the child return
steps.text: Offer watching or one easy step into play. No apology, explanation or repair is required first. Later, when ready, help put things right. Another child need not accept affection.

steps.title: Review what adults did
steps.text: Write facts separately from guesses. Did adults make the planned change? Could the child ask for help and enjoy activities? Compare with the family and teacher; seek advice sooner if worries grow.

videos.title: How-to: 5 Steps for Brain-Building Serve and Return
videos.publisher: Center on the Developing Child at Harvard University
videos.summary: Adults notice what interests a child, respond and wait for another turn. For example, a child points to a toy; the adult names it and pauses. The child can answer through a gesture or sound. Speech and eye contact are not required. Examples involving children below 12 months are background only; this course’s practice starts at 12 months.
videos.prompt: Look for what the child does, how the adult answers and when the adult waits. Then describe a similar exchange using a gesture instead of speech.
videos.accessibility: The official page has explanatory text and several language options. You can use the summary here for the task without watching; player captions and availability may vary.
videos.verifiedHosting: Official Harvard page links to its YouTube player. The page and video title were verified; playback was not independently tested.

videos.title: The importance of emotions in the early years foundation stage framework
videos.summary: Adults discuss helping children feel safe, noticing feelings and giving them time. Examples include saying goodbye to a caregiver and wanting the same toy. Comfort and practical help come first; a conversation about solving the problem can wait until the child can join in.
videos.prompt: Find one moment for comfort now and one for teaching later. Give a practical change too, such as less waiting or fewer children around the toy.
videos.accessibility: A full transcript is on the official page below the Vimeo video. You can also use this course summary for the task.
videos.verifiedHosting: Official DfE page and linked Vimeo player verified. Player title: EYFS Personal, social and emotional development – Emotions.

videos.title: How Children and Adults Can Build Core Capabilities for Life
videos.publisher: Center on the Developing Child at Harvard University
videos.summary: This animation explains skills such as remembering a plan, waiting and changing approach. Practice can help these skills; stress can make them harder to use. The brain pictures illustrate ideas. They cannot tell you what is happening inside a particular child’s brain.
videos.prompt: Choose one way to make a task easier for the adult and child, such as giving one instruction instead of several. Describe the change you can see, rather than guessing a brain state.
videos.accessibility: The official page has a written summary and English and Japanese video options. You can use the summary here for the task without watching.
videos.verifiedHosting: Official Harvard page verifies title and five-minute duration and links to its YouTube player; playback was not independently tested.

videos.title: Having Big Feelings: Healthy Minds, Thriving Kids Pre-K
videos.summary: This episode is made for children aged 3–5; the optional course task is for adults. Main message: big feelings are allowed and a trusted adult can help. Try familiar ways to feel more comfortable during easy moments. Asking through a gesture or device counts, and no calming technique is compulsory.
videos.prompt: Choose one activity shown and say how you would offer it. Then explain what you would do if the child declined, and when you could practise later without pressure. Do not require breathing, speech or touch.
videos.accessibility: The official page links free resources for educators and caregivers. You can use this course summary for the adult task without watching. Playback and captions were not independently tested.
videos.verifiedHosting: Official Child Mind Institute episode page, linked YouTube player and displayed 6:26 duration verified on 6 October 2026. Companion educator materials were read; playback was not independently tested.

videos.title: Helping toddlers learn about feelings
videos.publisher: Raising Children Network; My Toddler and Me series from Karitane and UNSW
videos.durationLabel: Short toddler feelings video; optional adult viewing
videos.summary: A toddler may want closeness one moment and space the next. If they push an offered hand away, stop the touch and stay available: “I can sit here.” Watch their response. Save explanation or practice for a moment when they can join in.
videos.prompt: Compare the example with Priya’s arrival. Practise a few words you could use if she declines touch. Show where you would stay so she has space and you can still help.
videos.accessibility: A full transcript is available on the official page and was read. You can also use this summary for the task. Playback and captions were not independently tested.
videos.verifiedHosting: Official Raising Children Network page, transcript and Karitane/UNSW attribution verified on 6 October 2026. The video is republished with permission; no exact runtime is asserted.

sources.title: Preschool Promise Child Assessments Technical Report 2017–2018
sources.publisher: Mary Fuhs, University of Dayton (September 2018); linked by Conscious Discipline

This observational evaluation is not a randomised test of each practice, a trial of this course or proof of a brain mechanism.

evidenceNotes.title: Professional guidance and original classroom applications
evidenceNotes.text: ZERO TO THREE, Child Mind Institute, NCPMI, Harvard’s activity resources and Raising Children Network offer professional explanations, synthesis and practical examples. They inform the taught adult decisions, but do not constitute trials of these scripts, games or tools. All course scenarios, wording and tool layouts are original; no provider endorses the course.

evidenceNotes.title: Branded materials are examples, not independent proof
evidenceNotes.text: Conscious Discipline is a named educational programme. Selected resources inform reflection on predictability, adult-supported spaces and feelings vocabulary. Its branded steps, characters and brain-state explanations are not adopted as a diagnostic framework or copied into the course. Child Mind’s Pre-K materials are also identified as a programme, not represented as an independent evaluation of this training. Free access does not mean unrestricted reuse.

evidenceNotes.title: Independent research and limits of inference
evidenceNotes.text: EEF’s evidence synthesis and research agenda address the wider evidence base separately from provider practice materials. The early-years intervention evidence remains limited and uneven; co-regulation-specific and younger-child evidence has gaps. A Conscious Discipline-linked report describes an adjusted observational association in 45 classrooms, not a randomised test of individual practices. None of these sources independently validates this 75-minute course, guarantees an outcome or establishes a neural effect from a script.

evidenceNotes.title: Local safety and individual judgement remain essential
evidenceNotes.text: Research-informed support for children from 12 months does not replace approved care procedures, individual communication plans, supervision, health assessment, emergency response or safeguarding. Some reference sources cover younger babies; these remain background rather than under-12-month practical assignments. Course age bands are broad planning guides, not milestone tests. The course excludes forced touch or gaze, withholding care, ignoring distress, improvised restrictive techniques and clinical treatment instructions.

evidenceNotes.title: Access, copyright and optional viewing
evidenceNotes.text: New provider pages and documents were checked on 6 October 2026. The new video additions were checked at page, companion-resource and transcript level; their playback was not independently tested. Each course video has an adult viewing task and text alternative. Conscious Discipline’s schedule download may require a free account. Provider graphics, stories, templates and logos are linked rather than reproduced or translated.
